claim: H. pylori colonizes the stomach in about half of the world's human population.
source: H. pylori colonizes the stomach in about half of the world's human population, and its presence in the stomach is the strongest known risk factor for gastric cancer (Uemura et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uemura et al., 2001

claim: H. pylori presence in the stomach is the strongest known risk factor for gastric cancer.
source: H. pylori colonizes the stomach in about half of the world's human population, and its presence in the stomach is the strongest known risk factor for gastric cancer (Uemura et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uemura et al., 2001

claim: H. pylori strains containing a cag PAI are associated with a significantly higher incidence of gastric cancer than strains lacking the cag PAI.
source: H. pylori strains containing a pathogenicity island (cag PAI), encoding CagA (a secreted effector protein) and the Cag T4SS, are associated with a significantly higher incidence of gastric cancer than that associated with strains lacking the cag PAI (Blaser et al., 1995; Cover, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blaser et al., 1995 and Cover, 2016

claim: Gastric cancer is the third leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide.
source: Gastric cancer is the third leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, and there are nearly one million new gastric carcinoma cases annually (Plummer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Plummer et al., 2016

claim: There are nearly one million new gastric carcinoma cases annually.
source: Gastric cancer is the third leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, and there are nearly one million new gastric carcinoma cases annually (Plummer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Plummer et al., 2016

claim: Bacterial T4SSs can mediate horizontal transfer of DNA among bacteria (conjugation).
source: Bacterial T4SSs are versatile molecular machines that can mediate a wide variety of functions, including horizontal transfer of DNA among bacteria (conjugation) and delivery of effector proteins into eukaryotic cells (Galán and Waksman, 2018; Grohmann et al., 2018; Waksman, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Galán and Waksman, 2018; Grohmann et al., 2018; Waksman, 2019

claim: Bacterial T4SSs can mediate delivery of effector proteins into eukaryotic cells.
source: Bacterial T4SSs are versatile molecular machines that can mediate a wide variety of functions, including horizontal transfer of DNA among bacteria (conjugation) and delivery of effector proteins into eukaryotic cells (Galán and Waksman, 2018; Grohmann et al., 2018; Waksman, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Galán and Waksman, 2018; Grohmann et al., 2018; Waksman, 2019

claim: T4SSs in Gram-negative bacteria are comprised of an inner membrane complex, a membrane-spanning core complex, and in some systems, an extracellular pilus.
source: T4SSs in Gram-negative bacteria are comprised of an inner membrane complex, a membrane-spanning core complex that extends from the inner membrane to the outer membrane, and in some systems, an extracellular pilus (Galán and Waksman, 2018; Grohmann et al., 2018; Waksman, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Galán and Waksman, 2018; Grohmann et al., 2018; Waksman, 2019

claim: Minimized T4SSs contain about 12 components (VirB1-11 and VirD4).
source: T4SSs vary in complexity, ranging from 'minimized' or 'prototype' systems that contain about 12 components (VirB1-11 and VirD4), as found in Agrobacterium tumefaciens, Xanthomonas citri, or conjugation systems, to expanded systems containing more than 20 components (Bhatty et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhatty et al., 2013

claim: Expanded T4SSs contain more than 20 components.
source: T4SSs vary in complexity, ranging from 'minimized' or 'prototype' systems that contain about 12 components (VirB1-11 and VirD4), as found in Agrobacterium tumefaciens, Xanthomonas citri, or conjugation systems, to expanded systems containing more than 20 components (Bhatty et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhatty et al., 2013

claim: Expanded T4SSs contain unique species-specific components.
source: Expanded T4SSs contain unique species-specific components and are much larger in size than their minimized counterparts.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: The Legionella Dot/Icm translocates more than 300 effector proteins.
source: The Legionella Dot/Icm translocates more than 300 effector proteins, thereby allowing intracellular bacterial replication (Qiu and Luo, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Qiu and Luo, 2017

claim: The H. pylori Cag T4SS is only known to deliver one effector protein, CagA.
source: In contrast, the H. pylori Cag T4SS is only known to deliver one effector protein, CagA (a bacterial oncoprotein), into gastric cells, resulting in altered cell signaling (Cover et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cover et al., 2020

claim: Minimized T4SS core complexes are typically ~250 Å in width and ~150 Å in height.
source: Structural studies of minimized T4SSs have revealed a core complex (typically ~250 Å in width and ~150 Å in height) that contains three proteins (VirB7, VirB9, and VirB10) (Chandran et al., 2009; Fronzes et al., 2009; Low et al., 2014; Sgro et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chandran et al., 2009; Fronzes et al., 2009; Low et al., 2014; Sgro et al., 2018

claim: Minimized T4SS core complexes contain three proteins (VirB7, VirB9, and VirB10).
source: Structural studies of minimized T4SSs have revealed a core complex (typically ~250 Å in width and ~150 Å in height) that contains three proteins (VirB7, VirB9, and VirB10) (Chandran et al., 2009; Fronzes et al., 2009; Low et al., 2014; Sgro et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chandran et al., 2009; Fronzes et al., 2009; Low et al., 2014; Sgro et al., 2018

claim: The H. pylori Cag T4SS core complex is ~400 Å in width and ~250 Å in height.
source: The H. pylori Cag T4SS core complex is a much larger mushroom-shaped assembly (~400 Å in width and ~250 Å in height) that contains structural homologs of the proteins found in minimized systems [CagT (VirB7), CagX (VirB9), and CagY (VirB10)] along with additional proteins (Cag3 and CagM) that lack homologs in other bacterial species (Chung et al., 2019; Frick-Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chung et al., 2019; Frick-Cheng et al., 2016

claim: The H. pylori Cag T4SS core complex contains CagT (VirB7 homolog), CagX (VirB9 homolog), and CagY (VirB10 homolog).
source: The H. pylori Cag T4SS core complex is a much larger mushroom-shaped assembly (~400 Å in width and ~250 Å in height) that contains structural homologs of the proteins found in minimized systems [CagT (VirB7), CagX (VirB9), and CagY (VirB10)] along with additional proteins (Cag3 and CagM) that lack homologs in other bacterial species (Chung et al., 2019; Frick-Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chung et al., 2019; Frick-Cheng et al., 2016

claim: Cag3 and CagM lack homologs in other bacterial species.
source: The H. pylori Cag T4SS core complex is a much larger mushroom-shaped assembly (~400 Å in width and ~250 Å in height) that contains structural homologs of the proteins found in minimized systems [CagT (VirB7), CagX (VirB9), and CagY (VirB10)] along with additional proteins (Cag3 and CagM) that lack homologs in other bacterial species (Chung et al., 2019; Frick-Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chung et al., 2019; Frick-Cheng et al., 2016

claim: The Cag T4SS core complex consists of an outer membrane cap (OMC), a periplasmic ring (PR), and a stalk.
source: The Cag T4SS core complex has been described as consisting of three distinct structural features: the outer membrane cap (OMC) consisting of an outer-layer (O-layer) and inner-layer (I-layer), a periplasmic ring (PR), and a stalk (Chang et al., 2018; Chung et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang et al., 2018; Chung et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2019

claim: There is a symmetry mismatch between the 14-fold-symmetric OMC and the 17-fold symmetric PR.
source: There is an apparent symmetry mismatch between the 14-fold-symmetric OMC and the 17-fold symmetric PR (Figure 1a; Chung et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 1a

claim: Central portions of the OMC are composed of CagT, CagX, and CagY.
source: Our recent sub-4Å structure of the Cag T4SS revealed that central portions of the OMC are composed of CagT, CagX, and CagY (VirB7, VirB9, and VirB10 homologs), but the resolution of the map did not allow us to build molecular models for the entire complex (Chung et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2019

claim: Peripheral regions of the OMC are missing in the ΔCag3 Cag T4SS map.
source: When comparing the maps reconstructed from the WT and Δcag3 strains, peripheral components of the O-layer of the OMC are missing in the Δcag3 map.
evidence: Direct comparison of cryo-EM maps from WT and Δcag3 strains

claim: At least a portion of the peripheral density missing in the Δcag3 map is likely composed of Cag3.
source: At least a portion of this peripheral density is likely composed of Cag3, since it is the component most notably absent in core complex preparations from the Δcag3 mutant [based on SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)].
evidence: Supported by SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: The PR remained intact in the Δcag3 map.
source: Notably, the PR remained intact in the Δcag3 map, and weak density was still observed within the I-layer (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: Observation from cryo-EM map shown in Figure 1b,c

claim: Two copies of CagT (CagT-1 and CagT-2) are present in the OMC asymmetric unit.
source: Positioned adjacent and peripheral to the previously described CagT (CagT-1), we identified another copy of CagT which we call CagT-2 (Figures 2a,b and 3a).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figures 2a,b and 3a

claim: The two copies of CagT differ significantly in the conformations of both their N- and C-termini.
source: We found that the two copies of CagT differ significantly in the conformations of both their N- and C-termini (Figure 4a).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4a

claim: The N-terminus of CagT-2 forms a β-strand that completes a β-sheet within Cag3-1.
source: Within CagT-2, the N-terminus adopts a different conformation, one in which it is wrapped back around the central, globular VirB7-like fold, forming a β-strand that completes a β-sheet within an adjacent protein that we designate as Cag3-1 (Figure 4c–f, Video 2).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4c–f and Video 2

claim: A putative lipidation site (C21) in both CagT-1 and CagT-2 is placed in close proximity to the outer membrane.
source: Despite the structural differences between CagT-1 and CagT-2, a putative lipidation site (C21) in both proteins (McClain et al., 2020) is placed in close proximity to the outer membrane (Figure 4g).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4g, with citation to McClain et al., 2020

claim: The C-terminal α-helices of CagT-1 and CagT-2 adopt different conformations and contact different proteins.
source: The C-termini of both CagT molecules adopt extended conformations that differ in their overall direction and organization. In CagT-1, the C-terminal α-helices extend outward from the center of the map, forming contacts with CagT-1 Cag3-1, Cag3-2, and Cag3-4 within the OMC (Figure 4h; Chung et al., 2019). Conversely, the C-terminal α-helices of CagT-2 are connected by an apparently dynamic linker and are arranged such that they contact a distinct repertoire of OMC proteins, including Cag3-1, Cag3-2, and CagM-1 (Figure 4i).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4h,i

claim: The C-terminal α-helical extensions of CagT are critical to maintaining the expanded architecture of the Cag T4SS OMC.
source: Because of this, we suggest that the addition of these C-terminal α-helices is critical to maintaining the expanded architecture of the Cag T4SS OMC, as it has been previously shown that Cag3 cannot be effectively incorporated into core complexes lacking CagT (Frick-Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference based on structural data and citation to Frick-Cheng et al., 2016

claim: Cag3 cannot be effectively incorporated into core complexes lacking CagT.
source: Because of this, we suggest that the addition of these C-terminal α-helices is critical to maintaining the expanded architecture of the Cag T4SS OMC, as it has been previously shown that Cag3 cannot be effectively incorporated into core complexes lacking CagT (Frick-Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frick-Cheng et al., 2016

claim: The C-terminal α-helices of CagT-1 adopt an inward-folded conformation in the Δcag3 OMC reconstruction.
source: The orientation of the CagT-1 C-terminal α-helices differs significantly in the Δcag3 OMC reconstruction compared to their orientation in the wild-type OMC reconstruction. In contrast to the extended conformation of the CagT-1 α-helices in the WT OMC, in the Δcag3 OMC these helices are folded inward and pack against α-helices of CagX and CagY within the central chamber (Figures 2c,d and 5a, Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figures 2c,d, 5a, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2b

claim: No density for CagT-2 is observed in the Δcag3 map.
source: In addition to the loss of peripheral density corresponding to Cag3 within the Δcag3 map, we observe no density for CagT-2 in the Δcag3 map.
evidence: Observation from cryo-EM data

claim: CagT-2 cannot effectively fold when Cag3 is absent, leading to dissociation or unfolding.
source: One possible explanation for the loss of CagT-2 is that it cannot effectively fold when Cag3 is absent, leading to dissociation of the complex or unfolding of the protein.
evidence: Speculation based on structural observations

claim: CagX and CagY adopt nearly identical conformations in the ∆Cag3 mutant core complex when compared to the WT structure.
source: CagX and CagY adopt nearly identical conformations in the ∆Cag3 mutant core complex when compared to the WT structure (RMSDs of 0.5 Å and 0.3 Å, respectively) (Figure 5b,c).
evidence: Structural comparison with RMSD values shown in Figure 5b,c

claim: Assembly of the Cag T4SS is initiated by positioning CagX and CagY in association with the outer membrane.
source: This is consistent with a proposal that assembly of the Cag T4SS is initiated by positioning CagX and CagY in association with the outer membrane (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2019

claim: Five copies of Cag3 are present within each asymmetric unit of the OMC.
source: Further analysis revealed five copies of Cag3 within each asymmetric unit (named Cag3-1 through Cag3-5, based on their proximity to the central channel) (Figure 2a,b Figure 3b).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2a,b and Figure 3b

claim: All five copies of Cag3 adopt similar core folds with RMSDs of 0.5–1.3 Å.
source: All five copies of Cag3 are found within the periphery of the OMC and adopt similar core folds (with RMSDs of 0.5–1.3 Å) that are connected via a highly interwoven architecture (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: Structural comparison with RMSD values shown in Figure 6a–c

claim: Cag3-1 contains two globular domains (proximal and distal) connected by a long loop.
source: The first copy of Cag3 (Cag3-1) contains the longest uninterrupted span of density (corresponding to residues 62–308) and consists of two globular domains (proximal and distal) connected by a long loop, without an intramolecular interface (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 6a,b

claim: A loop in the proximal domain of Cag3-1 (residues 181–204) interacts with adjacent asymmetric units.
source: The proximal domain of Cag3-1 is positioned adjacent to CagT-2 within the center of the map and contains a loop (residues 181–204) that interacts with adjacent asymmetric units (Figure 6g).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 6g

claim: The loop in Cag3-1 (residues 181–204) may act as a lynchpin during assembly.
source: We predict that this loop may act as a lynchpin during assembly, since it forms the most extensive network of contacts within the center of the complex.
evidence: Inference based on structural observations

claim: The proximal domain of Cag3-1 contains a core fold similar to CagT and X. citri VirB7.
source: Notably, the proximal domain of Cag3-1 consists of a 'core' fold that is similar to a corresponding fold in CagT and the related VirB7 homolog from X. citri (Figure 6h; Sgro et al., 2018).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 6h with citation to Sgro et al., 2018

claim: A portion of CagM (residues 187–366) was modeled into peripheral density within the I-layer.
source: We modeled a portion of CagM (residues 187–366) into peripheral density within the I-layer and observe an α-helical fold with two sub-domains: a 3-helix bundle at the N-terminus connected by a short loop to a 5-helix fold at the C-terminus.
evidence: Model building based on cryo-EM density

claim: Two copies of CagM (CagM-1 and CagM-2) are present within the I-layer of the OMC.
source: We also observe a second helical fold containing 9 α-helices, arranged in a nearly identical fashion as in CagM-1 within the center of the I-layer, albeit at lower resolution (Figure 7b). We fit the CagM sequence into this density and note that the refined structure (designated CagM-2) again contains two subdomains connected via a flexible hinge (Figure 7c).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 7b,c

claim: The OMC proteins exist at a stoichiometry of 1:1:2:2:5 (CagX:CagY:CagM:CagT:Cag3).
source: Based on these analyses, we conclude that the OMC proteins exist at a stoichiometry of 1:1:2:2:5 (CagX:CagY:CagM:CagT:Cag3).
evidence: Conclusion based on structural analysis of cryo-EM data

claim: The Cag T4SS OMC contains 70 copies of Cag3.
source: Illustrating this point, we note that the inclusion of 5 copies of Cag3 within the asymmetric unit results in 70 copies of Cag3 incorporated into the fully assembled Cag T4SS OMC.
evidence: Calculation based on 5 copies per asymmetric unit and 14-fold symmetry

claim: The Cag T4SS OMC contains 154 different polypeptide chains in total.
source: In total, the Cag T4SS OMC contains 154 different polypeptide chains.
evidence: Calculation based on stoichiometry and symmetry

claim: Prototype core complexes contain a total of 42 different polypeptide chains.
source: In comparison, prototype core complexes contain a total of 42 different polypeptide chains (14 copies each of VirB7, VirB9 and VirB10).
evidence: Calculation based on known stoichiometry of prototype systems

claim: The PR is mostly comprised of a globular domain formed by an N-terminal portion of CagX (residues 32–130, 261–323).
source: Because of this advance, it is possible to identify the two components of the PR as portions of CagX (residues 32–130, 261–323) and CagY (residues 1469–1603). The PR is mostly comprised of a globular domain formed by an N-terminal portion of CagX, which starts from the cytoplasm-facing side of the PR, wraps back and forth to form two β-sheets, and ends in an α-helix pointed towards the OMC (Figure 8a, Video 3).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 8a and Video 3

claim: The N-terminal domain of CagX is homologous to the N-terminal domain of X. citri VirB9 with an RMSD of 0.8 Å.
source: The N-terminal domain of CagX is homologous to the N-terminal domain of X. citri VirB9 (RMSD of 0.8 Å, PDB 6GYB) (Figure 8b–d; Sgro et al., 2018).
evidence: Structural comparison with RMSD value shown in Figure 8b–d, with citation to Sgro et al., 2018

claim: The C-terminal domain of CagX is highly similar to its X. citri counterpart with an RMSD of 0.6 Å.
source: The C-terminal domain of CagX is also highly similar to its X. citri counterpart (RMSD of 0.6 Å, PDB 6GYB) (Figure 8e,f).
evidence: Structural comparison with RMSD value shown in Figure 8e,f

claim: CagX contains an insertion that forms a long α-helix in the center of the molecule.
source: The major difference between the two proteins is the presence of an insertion within CagX that forms a long α-helix in the center of the molecule (Figure 8d,g).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 8d,g

claim: The N- and C-terminal domains of H. pylori CagX are positioned ~200 Å apart.
source: Because of this feature, the N- and C-terminal domains of H. pylori CagX are positioned ~200 Å apart (within the PR and OMC, respectively), whereas the corresponding domains of X. citri VirB9 are ~80 Å apart (Figure 8h).
evidence: Structural measurement shown in Figure 8h

claim: The corresponding domains of X. citri VirB9 are ~80 Å apart.
source: Because of this feature, the N- and C-terminal domains of H. pylori CagX are positioned ~200 Å apart (within the PR and OMC, respectively), whereas the corresponding domains of X. citri VirB9 are ~80 Å apart (Figure 8h).
evidence: Structural measurement shown in Figure 8h

claim: A segment of CagY within the PR (residues 1469–1603) adopts a highly elongated fold consisting of four α-helices.
source: Wrapped around the PR portion of CagX is a segment of CagY that starts from the cytoplasm-facing side of the PR and forms four α-helices that are connected by loops that vary in length (ranging from 3 to 41 residues) (Figure 8i).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 8i

claim: The CagX-CagY interface in H. pylori is much larger than the corresponding VirB9-VirB10 interface in X. citri.
source: The CagX-CagY interface in H. pylori is much larger than the corresponding VirB9-VirB10 interface, likely due to an expansion of CagY compared to VirB10 homologs in minimized systems (Figure 8j).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 8j

claim: CagX and CagY exist within both the OMC and PR.
source: The identification of CagX and CagY within the PR was unexpected, as it suggests that each protein exists within both the OMC and PR, two distinct regions of the T4SS that differ in overall symmetry (Figure 9a).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 9a

claim: The long helical expansion within CagX appears to bridge the OMC and PR.
source: Although we cannot specifically trace either component across the symmetry mismatch, we note that the long helical expansion within CagX appears to bridge the OMC and PR.
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data

claim: 14 tubes of helical density connect the OMC and PR.
source: This model is supported by focused refinement of the connecting region between the OMC and PR in the WT map without imposition of symmetry, which shows 14 tubes of helical density connecting the OMC and PR (Figure 9b).
evidence: Structural observation from focused refinement shown in Figure 9b

claim: Only 14 copies of CagX within the PR appear to traverse the symmetry mismatch.
source: Notably, only 14 copies of CagX within the PR appear to traverse the symmetry mismatch, leaving three domains within the PR without an obvious connection to the OMC (Figure 9c, Video 4).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data shown in Figure 9c and Video 4

claim: The structural conservation between central domains of CagT and Cag3 could not have been predicted based on sequence comparisons alone.
source: A notable discovery is the structural conservation between central domains of CagT and Cag3, a result which could not have been predicted based on sequence comparisons alone.
evidence: Conclusion based on structural analysis

claim: Interactions between Cag3-Cag3, Cag3-CagT, Cag3-CagM, CagX-CagM, and CagT-CagM were previously detected using yeast two-hybrid screening or studies of recombinant proteins.
source: Specifically, interactions between Cag3-Cag3, Cag3-CagT, Cag3-CagM, CagX-CagM, and CagT-CagM were previous detected using a yeast two-hybrid screening approach or by studies of recombinant proteins produced in E. coli, and are consistent with the structural observations reported here (Busler et al., 2006; Kutter et al., 2008; Smart et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Busler et al., 2006; Kutter et al., 2008; Smart et al., 2017

claim: CagX and CagY assemble to form portions of both the OMC and PR, bridging the symmetry mismatch.
source: We show that CagX and CagY assemble to form portions of both the OMC and PR, bridging the previously described symmetry mismatch within the core complex (Chung et al., 2019).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM data with citation to Chung et al., 2019

claim: A similar phenomenon of proteins bridging symmetry mismatch has been detected in the Type Three Secretion System of Salmonella.
source: Although the existence of CagX and CagY in both the OMC and PR seems inconsistent with the observed symmetry mismatch, it should be noted that this is not the first example of such a phenomenon. Indeed, a similar phenomenon has been detected in the Type Three Secretion System (T3SS) of Salmonella, in which one molecule (InvG) exists on both sides of a C15-C16 symmetry mismatch (Hu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2018

claim: Symmetry mismatch has been observed in multiple types of bacterial secretion systems.
source: Symmetry mismatch has been observed in multiple types of bacterial secretion systems or other large bacterial machines, including T2SSs, T3SSs, the L. pneumophila Dot/Icm T4SS, T6SSs, and the Salmonella flagellar motor (Chernyatina and Low, 2019; Dix et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020), suggesting an important physiological function for this architecture.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chernyatina and Low, 2019; Dix et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020

claim: No symmetry mismatch has been observed in core complexes of minimized T4SS systems such as the X. citri T4SS.
source: Interestingly, no symmetry mismatch has been observed in core complexes of minimized T4SS systems such as the X. citri T4SS, which contain 14 copies of both the N-terminal and C-terminal domains of VirB9 (Sgro et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sgro et al., 2018

claim: The Cag T4SS core complex is much larger in size than core complexes in prototype systems.
source: When comparing the H. pylori Cag T4SS core complex to corresponding T4SS subassemblies in other species, there are striking differences. Most notably, the Cag T4SS core complex is much larger in size than core complexes in prototype systems, and it contains two species-specific components (Cag3 and CagM).
evidence: Comparison based on structural data

claim: The portions of CagX and CagY within the PR are similar to the parts of VirB9 and VirB10 which reside in the I-layer of the X. citri T4SS.
source: In the current study, we discovered that the portions of CagX and CagY within the PR are similar to the parts of VirB9 and VirB10 which reside in the I-layer of the X. citri T4SS (Sgro et al., 2018).
evidence: Structural comparison with citation to Sgro et al., 2018

claim: The I-layer within the X. citri T4SS is positioned ~115 Å below the outer membrane.
source: Second, the position of the X. citri T4SS I-layer within the OMC (~115 Å below the outer membrane, as determined by the position of the membrane spanning helices) is similar to that of the I-layer of the Cag T4SS (positioned ~120 Å beneath the outer membrane, and composed of CagM).
evidence: Structural measurement

claim: The I-layer of the Cag T4SS is positioned ~120 Å beneath the outer membrane.
source: Second, the position of the X. citri T4SS I-layer within the OMC (~115 Å below the outer membrane, as determined by the position of the membrane spanning helices) is similar to that of the I-layer of the Cag T4SS (positioned ~120 Å beneath the outer membrane, and composed of CagM).
evidence: Structural measurement

claim: Cryo-EM data for the wild-type complex achieved a resolution of 3.4 Å for the OMC with C14 symmetry.
source: Focused 3D classification and 3D refinement were used to determine higher resolution maps of the WT OMC (with 14-fold symmetry), resulting in a 3D map of the OMC (14-fold symmetry) at 3.4 Å.
evidence: Resolution reported from cryo-EM data processing

claim: Cryo-EM data for the ΔCag3 complex achieved a resolution of 3.1 Å for the OMC with C14 symmetry.
source: The maps of the OMC and PR were further refined using focused 3D refinement (with local refinement), resulting in 3D maps of the OMC (14-fold symmetry) and the PR (17-fold symmetry) at 3.1 Å and 3.0 Å, respectively.
evidence: Resolution reported from cryo-EM data processing

claim: Cryo-EM data for the ΔCag3 complex achieved a resolution of 3.0 Å for the PR with C17 symmetry.
source: The maps of the OMC and PR were further refined using focused 3D refinement (with local refinement), resulting in 3D maps of the OMC (14-fold symmetry) and the PR (17-fold symmetry) at 3.1 Å and 3.0 Å, respectively.
evidence: Resolution reported from cryo-EM data processing
